connection: Session 30 used constructor injection to replace a repository during tests. Session 30B now studies the runtime container that constructs services and controls instance reuse.
objectives: Identify the composition root as the place that chooses implementations and lifetimes.
Predict and observe transient, scoped, and singleton identity within and across scopes.
Explain why lifetime selection matters when objects hold mutable state.

visuals.title: The composition root is the assembly bench
visuals.explanation: Registrations gather in one deliberate place where the application chooses which concrete types satisfy requests and how long their instances live.

visuals.title: Transient creates a fresh ticket every time
visuals.explanation: Two resolutions, even inside one scope, return two different TransientMarker objects.

visuals.title: Scoped shares one tray per scope
visuals.explanation: Repeated resolutions inside the first scope reuse one ScopedMarker, while the second scope receives a different instance.

visuals.title: Singleton is one lighthouse for all scopes
visuals.explanation: Both scopes resolve the same SingletonMarker instance from the provider. Shared mutable state would therefore be shared across all consumers.

preQuiz.prompt: Where should an application normally choose implementations and lifetimes?
preQuiz.explanation: The composition root centralizes object-graph decisions.

preQuiz.prompt: What should two transient resolutions return?
options: The same instance in one scope
preQuiz.explanation: Transient creates a new instance for each resolution.

preQuiz.prompt: Which lifetime reuses one instance inside a scope but not across scopes?
preQuiz.explanation: Each scope owns one scoped instance.

concept.title: Constructor injection and a container are related but different
paragraphs: Session 30 passed a repository directly into ClockEntryService. That is constructor injection and does not require a container.

A DI container stores construction rules and builds object graphs. IServiceCollection holds registrations; BuildServiceProvider creates the resolver. The composition root is the application location that owns those choices.
concept.code:
ServiceCollection services = new();
using ServiceProvider provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();

concept.title: Transient means new per resolution
paragraphs: AddTransient registers a rule that creates a new instance whenever the service is requested.
ReferenceEquals compares object identity. Resolving TransientMarker twice from the same scope should therefore produce false.

concept.title: Scoped means one per scope
paragraphs: AddScoped reuses one instance within a single IServiceScope. A different scope receives a different instance.
This is useful when several operations should share context for one boundary, such as one web request, without sharing it globally.
concept.code:
// Same scope: true
// Different scopes: false

concept.title: Singleton means one per provider
paragraphs: AddSingleton returns the same instance across scopes created by one ServiceProvider.
Singletons require care with mutable state because all consumers can observe and change the same object. Lifetime is an ownership decision, not a performance decoration.

lab.title: Observe Three DI Lifetimes
lab.objective: Register, resolve, and compare transient, scoped, and singleton instances in two explicit scopes.
lab.task: Print four identity comparisons whose true and false results prove each lifetime rule.
lab.startingCondition: Session 30 completed isolated service tests. The learner ScratchPad has no Session30B experiment and does not yet reference Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.

steps.text: In the ScratchPad project, create folder Session30B and file Session30B/LifetimeExperiments.cs. Add using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection and declare public sealed class LifetimeExperiments.
Inside LifetimeExperiments, add public void Run. Create ServiceCollection services inside Run. This method is the experiment's composition root because it will choose registrations and lifetimes.
steps.purposeAfter: You now have the one place that will assemble this experiment's object graph. Next you will register three types with three different reuse rules before resolving anything.

steps.text: Inside Run, register TransientMarker with AddTransient, ScopedMarker with AddScoped, and SingletonMarker with AddSingleton. Read each call as: register this service type with this reuse rule.

Inside the class but outside Run, add private sealed marker classes named TransientMarker, ScopedMarker, and SingletonMarker. They intentionally have no behavior so object identity is the only changing variable.
Build the ScratchPad project in Release before adding provider and scope code.
steps.purposeAfter: The registrations and marker types now compile. Building the provider next will turn those descriptions into a resolver that owns created instances.

steps.text: At the end of Run, build ServiceProvider from services with a using declaration. Then create firstScope and secondScope as two using declarations. The provider and scopes are disposable owners.

Inside the class but outside Run, add private static T Resolve<T>(IServiceScope scope) where T : notnull. Return scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<T>(). This helper keeps each identity comparison readable.
In Run, resolve TransientMarker twice from firstScope into two named variables. Print Transient reused in one scope followed by ReferenceEquals for those variables. Predict false before running.
steps.purposeAfter: The first comparison asks whether one scope changes the transient rule. It should not: each resolution creates a new object, so the next comparisons can contrast scoped reuse.

steps.text: Resolve ScopedMarker twice from firstScope. Print Scoped reused in one scope followed by ReferenceEquals. Predict true because one scope owns one scoped instance.
Resolve one ScopedMarker from firstScope and one from secondScope. Print Scoped reused across scopes followed by ReferenceEquals. Predict false because each scope owns a different scoped instance.
Resolve SingletonMarker once from each scope. Print Singleton reused across scopes followed by ReferenceEquals. Predict true because the provider owns one singleton instance.
steps.purposeAfter: All three lifetime rules are now represented by explicit identity evidence: transient false, scoped true then false, and singleton true. The experiment needs a caller so ScratchPad can display those predictions as observable results.

steps.text: In ScratchPad Program.cs after earlier session calls, print a Session 30B heading, create LifetimeExperiments, and call Run. Preserve all earlier experiments. Then run ScratchPad and verify the four predicted booleans.
steps.purposeAfter: The focused run proves instance reuse rather than merely describing registrations. The final validation now checks that adding the package and experiment did not damage the cumulative solution.

steps.text: Build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln in Release and run the complete test suite with --no-build. Open Solution Reveal only after both pass.
steps.code:
dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release
dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

reveals.title: Solution
reveals.text: The complete experiment gives each lifetime its own named resolution and predicted identity result.

lab.expectedBehavior:
Transient reused in one scope: False
Scoped reused in one scope: True
Scoped reused across scopes: False
Singleton reused across scopes: True
lab.validation: dotnet run --project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad.csproj --configuration Release && dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

review: The experiment stays in permanent ScratchPad rather than changing production registrations.
Each lifetime has a separate named identity comparison and predicted result.
The provider and both scopes are deterministically disposed.
No mocks, repositories, EF Core, HTTP, or async work is introduced.

options: To distinguish reuse within a scope from reuse across scopes
postQuiz.explanation: Scoped identity changes only when the scope boundary changes.

postQuiz.prompt: Why can singleton mutable state be risky?
options: All consumers share the same instance
postQuiz.explanation: One shared instance means shared mutations and concurrency responsibilities.

options: No, callers can construct and pass dependencies directly
postQuiz.explanation: A container automates construction; constructor injection itself is a class design.

reflections: Which code is the composition root of this experiment?
Why does scoped require two separate comparisons?
When would shared singleton state be intentional, and what safeguards would it need?
whatBreaks: Removing the second scope makes across-scope behavior impossible to observe. Replacing named resolutions with one compressed expression hides which instance belongs to which boundary. Omitting disposal loses explicit ownership of provider-created resources.
summary: A DI container applies construction and lifetime rules chosen at a composition root. Transient creates per resolution, scoped reuses within one scope, and singleton reuses across scopes owned by one provider. ReferenceEquals makes those ownership rules visible.
